questions.stem:
Statement: 'Parents, enroll your child in our reading programme — children who read regularly score better in school.'
Assumption I: Regular reading has a positive effect on a child's academic performance.
Assumption II: All parents universally want higher academic scores for their children.
Which assumption(s) is/are implicit in the statement?

options.option_text: Only Assumption I is implicit in the statement
Only Assumption II is implicit in the statement
Both Assumptions I and II are implicit in the statement
Neither Assumption I nor Assumption II is implicit here

questions.explanation: A is correct. The programme's claim that 'reading regularly leads to better scores' directly rests on the belief that reading improves academic performance — Assumption I is implicit without it the programme's promise is meaningless. Assumption II uses 'all parents universally', which is far too sweeping; the statement targets only parents who choose to enroll, not every parent. Key rule: whenever an assumption uses absolute language (all, every, only), verify whether the statement truly requires that absolute claim — it rarely does.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Install smoke detectors on every floor of your home to protect your family from fire hazards.'
Assumption I: Smoke detectors can provide early warning of fire, giving residents time to take protective action.
Assumption II: Fire hazards occur frequently in most residential homes.
Which assumption(s) is/are implicit?

options.option_text: Only Assumption I is implicit in the statement
Only Assumption II is implicit in the statement
Both Assumptions I and II are implicit in the statement
Neither Assumption I nor Assumption II is implicit here

questions.explanation: A is correct. The advice to install smoke detectors 'to protect from fire hazards' presupposes they actually protect — Assumption I is implicit, as without it the advice has no logic. Assumption II claims fires are frequent in most homes; but the statement is a precaution against the possibility of fire, not a statistical claim about its frequency. Trap alert: students confuse 'this danger can happen' (what the statement assumes) with 'this danger is common' (what Assumption II claims). A precautionary statement does not assume the threat is frequent.

questions.stem:
Statement: The city library has extended its operating hours to midnight on weekdays to help working professionals access books and study material.
Assumption I: Working professionals find it difficult to visit the library during regular daytime hours.
Assumption II: Accessing books and study material is the only purpose that a public library serves.
Which assumption(s) is/are implicit?

options.option_text: Only Assumption I is implicit in the statement
Only Assumption II is implicit in the statement
Both Assumptions I and II are implicit in the statement
Neither Assumption I nor Assumption II is implicit here

questions.explanation: A is correct. Extending hours specifically 'for working professionals' implies the library assumes they cannot come during regular hours — Assumption I is implicit, as without it the extension has no identified rationale. Assumption II narrows all library purposes to one, which the statement never claims. The library extended hours for one group to access one type of content; this says nothing about what other purposes libraries serve. Avoid accepting assumptions that use restrictive words like 'only' unless the statement itself is explicitly exclusive.

questions.stem:
Statement: A scientist has advised people living near mobile towers to limit electromagnetic radiation exposure by keeping their windows closed at night.
Assumption I: Prolonged exposure to radiation from mobile towers may have adverse health effects.
Assumption II: Closing windows at night can meaningfully reduce the electromagnetic radiation entering homes.
Which assumption(s) is/are implicit?

options.option_text: Only Assumption I is implicit in the statement
Only Assumption II is implicit in the statement
Both Assumptions I and II are implicit in the statement
Neither Assumption I nor Assumption II is implicit here

questions.explanation: C is correct. Assumption I: advising people to 'limit exposure' presupposes a health risk from that exposure — otherwise limiting it would be pointless (implicit). Assumption II: recommending the specific act of closing windows presupposes this action actually reduces radiation indoors — without this, the advice is useless (implicit). Both are load-bearing pillars of the advice. Contrast with Q2 where only the device's effectiveness was assumed: here, BOTH the existence of the risk AND the effectiveness of the specific remedy must be assumed for the statement to be rational.

questions.stem:
Statement: Employees are advised to submit travel reimbursement claims within 30 days of completing any official trip.
Assumption I: Without a deadline, employees may delay or forget to submit reimbursement claims.
Assumption II: The organisation has a budget allocated to fund employee travel reimbursements.
Assumption III: Every employee in the organisation undertakes official trips as part of their role.
Which of the following is correct?

options.option_text: Only Assumptions I and II are implicit in the statement
Only Assumptions I and III are implicit in the statement
Only Assumptions II and III are implicit in the statement
All three Assumptions I, II, and III are implicit here

questions.explanation: A is correct. Assumption I: setting a 30-day deadline implies the organisation foresees that without one, timely claims may not happen — implicit. Assumption II: advising submission of reimbursements implies a reimbursement system and budget exist; you cannot advise people to claim what the organisation has not set aside — implicit. Assumption III is NOT implicit: the advisory says 'employees completing official trips', which addresses those who travel; it does not assume every employee undertakes trips. Hard-case trap: the word 'employees' tempts students into inferring 'all employees travel', but the statement is conditional on trip completion, not universal.

questions.stem:
Statement: The railway ministry has directed that every railway station must have at least one platform fully accessible to persons with disabilities, equipped with ramps, tactile paths, and accessible restrooms.
Assumption I: Persons with disabilities currently face barriers in accessing railway platforms.
Assumption II: Ramps, tactile paths, and accessible restrooms fully address all mobility requirements of persons with disabilities.
Assumption III: Railway authorities are capable of implementing these modifications across all stations.
Which assumptions are implicit?

options.option_text: Only Assumptions I and III are implicit in the statement
Only Assumptions I and II are implicit in the statement
Only Assumption III is implicit in the statement
All Assumptions I, II, and III are implicit in the statement

questions.explanation: A is correct. Assumption I: a directive to make platforms accessible implies current inaccessibility — the directive would be redundant if platforms were already accessible (implicit). Assumption III: directing authorities to implement modifications implies the ministry believes they are capable of doing so — rational instructions presuppose feasibility (implicit). Assumption II is NOT implicit: the statement mandates specific features but never claims they 'fully address ALL mobility requirements' — that is an extreme inference beyond what the directive states. Key rule for hard questions: a directive assumes necessity (I) and feasibility (III), but it does NOT assume completeness or perfection of the prescribed solution.

questions.stem:
Statement: A technology firm has announced it will hire only candidates who possess at least one industry-recognised certification in addition to an academic degree.
Assumption I: Industry-recognised certifications signal practical competence beyond what academic degrees alone convey.
Assumption II: All industry-recognised certifications are regarded as equally valuable by the company.
Assumption III: Some candidates with relevant academic degrees may not hold any industry-recognised certification.
Which assumptions are implicit in the statement?

options.option_text: Only Assumptions I and III are implicit in the statement
Only Assumptions I and II are implicit in the statement
Only Assumption III is implicit in the statement
Only Assumptions II and III are implicit in the statement

questions.explanation: A is correct. Assumption I: adding a certification requirement on top of a degree implies the company believes certifications offer something degrees do not — otherwise why add the requirement at all? (implicit). Assumption III: the policy makes sense only if there exist degree-holders who lack certifications — if everyone already had one, the policy would screen nobody out and be pointless (implicit). Assumption II is NOT implicit: the firm requires 'at least one recognised certification' but does not treat all certifications as equal in worth; requiring any one certification does not presuppose parity among all certifications. The hard discriminating step: Assumption I is about why certifications matter at all; Assumption II is about relative value among them — the statement implies the former but is silent on the latter.
